topic: multilingual code generation; benchmark validity; test adequacy
status: bounded cross-paper lead; global novelty unconfirmed
claim: The audited evidence supports a testable concern that multilingual code-generation comparisons can depend on benchmark translation, prompt decisions, and test strength. MultiPL-E itself reports prompt sensitivity and language/task adaptation choices; EvalPlus later shows that greatly expanding HumanEval tests can expose previously passing incorrect code and reverse some model rankings in Python. This does not show that MultiPL-E's reported rankings are wrong: whether stronger tests or reasonable translation variants materially change cross-language conclusions remains unmeasured here.
positive_evidence: MultiPL-E evaluates HumanEval/MBPP translations in 18 additional languages with hidden unit tests and three models; it explicitly discusses benchmark representativeness, prompt choices, language-specific translation/type constraints, and limited item exclusions/modifications.

EvalPlus (arXiv:2305.01210) expands HumanEval tests 80-fold, reports pass@k reductions of up to 19.3–28.9% in evaluated settings, and describes ranking reversals; it is direct evidence that test adequacy can affect codegen conclusions, but not a multilingual MultiPL-E replication.

LiveCodeBench (arXiv:2403.07974) uses newly collected contest problems and evaluates code-related capabilities beyond generation, supporting benchmark freshness and task scope as separate design choices.
counterevidence: MultiPL-E is a careful extensible benchmark with executable tests, explicit adaptation procedures, and sensitivity analyses; configuration dependence does not invalidate its conditional findings.
EvalPlus evaluates HumanEval, not the translated MultiPL-E tasks or the same cross-language model ranking question.
LiveCodeBench is not a matched multilingual replication and cannot establish that language-by-language rank orders change.

falsifiable_test: On a preregistered set of at least 8 programming languages spanning typed/dynamic and high/low corpus-frequency groups, construct matched translations of the same tasks. For each language, compare the original unit tests with a substantially strengthened, independently reviewed test suite; separately vary plausible prompt/comment/type-annotation choices. Evaluate a fixed, version-pinned set of code models using paired prompts and common sampling budgets. Report per-language pass@k deltas, calibration, test mutation adequacy, and rank correlations/top-k rank changes with uncertainty. The lead weakens if language-specific scores and cross-language conclusions remain stable under stronger tests and reasonable prompt/translation variants.
limitations: Only one sampled multilingual benchmark paper was audited in this cell; EvalPlus and LiveCodeBench are targeted literature follow-ups, not sampled-frame observations and not independently reproduced here. The result is a hypothesis for a direct experiment, not a novelty or invalidity claim.

topic: code models; interpretability; probing; functional correctness
status: bounded validation question; global novelty unconfirmed
claim: The sampled DeepCodeProbe study and related syntax-probing papers show that syntactic structure can be recovered from code-model representations, while DeepCodeProbe itself identifies construct-validity and external-validity threats. The audited evidence does not establish whether probe scores predict executable correctness, security, or held-out maintenance outcomes—especially for current transformer LLMs. The actionable question is predictive validity, not whether syntax-probing papers exist.
positive_evidence: DeepCodeProbe probes four non-transformer maintenance architectures and reports abstract syntax representations, using trained/random model comparisons and clone/non-clone validation.
AST-Probe (arXiv:2206.11719) reports recovering AST structure from hidden representations across five pretrained models; this is counterevidence to claiming syntactic probing is unexplored.

A seven-model syntax/semantics probing study (arXiv:2212.10017) reports syntax strengths and more variable semantic representations, motivating separation of representational recovery from task competence.
counterevidence: DeepCodeProbe includes construct-validity checks and a replication package; the probe is not wholly unvalidated.
Prior and subsequent papers have probed syntax and semantics, so the broad topic is established.

The current evidence set does not include a direct controlled test relating probe scores to independently held-out functional outcomes; absence in this small audited set is not evidence the broader literature lacks such tests.

falsifiable_test: For several current transformer and non-transformer code models, compute preregistered syntax/semantic probe scores and evaluate the same models on held-out executable correctness, vulnerability detection, and maintenance tasks across multiple languages/projects. Control model size, training-data exposure, probe capacity, and task overlap; compare whether probe scores add calibrated predictive value beyond baseline model/task covariates and whether prediction transfers to held-out projects/languages. The lead weakens if probe scores add no stable out-of-sample predictive value, or is partly answered if strong transferable prediction already exists in prior work.
limitations: This is a research question derived from one sampled full text and targeted abstract/full-paper-level literature discovery; no model experiment was run and no systematic novelty search was completed. Interpretability, predictive validity, and causal explanation are distinct claims.

topic: software vulnerability detection; project and language transfer
status: bounded replication/design implication; not a new gap claim
claim: The sampled 2024 Java study reports a useful within-study bag-of-words/random-forest baseline and uneven cross-project transfer: at the 0.8 precision-and-recall threshold it reports an average of 1.4 targets for single-project training and 5/15 targets for train-on-14/test-on-one Android projects. Prior cross-project domain adaptation and C-to-Java transfer papers establish that transfer has already been studied. The defensible next step is comparable leakage-resistant evaluation under project/language shift, not claiming transfer is undiscovered.
positive_evidence: The sampled study compares 17 Java projects and reports its simple feature/model baseline; it explicitly runs train-one/predict-many and train-many/predict-one tests.
The train-one results are low at the 0.8 precision-and-recall threshold; pooling 14 Android projects increases the number of target projects meeting that threshold to five.
Prior work such as arXiv:2209.10406 studies cross-project vulnerability detection with domain adaptation; arXiv:2303.06177 studies vulnerability knowledge transfer from C to Java.
counterevidence: Some held-out Android targets meet the 0.8 threshold and the paper reports 10/15 at a 0.7 threshold; transfer is not uniformly absent.
The domain-adaptation and cross-language papers report positive transfer results under their own datasets and procedures, so poor transfer is not a universal conclusion.
The sampled study's authors identify project-count, Java-only, and inherited-label limitations; observed scores cannot be treated as unbiased production precision/recall.

falsifiable_test: Build a versioned benchmark from multiple Java and C/C++ projects with commit-level vulnerability labels reviewed independently. Deduplicate clones and near-duplicates before splitting; use temporal, project-held-out, and language-held-out evaluation. Compare single-project, pooled-project, and domain-adaptation methods at fixed false-positive budgets, with calibration, per-project confidence intervals, label-audit sensitivity, and performance under class prevalence shifts. The design implication is weakened if existing reproducible datasets already implement these controls and show stable transfer across held-out projects/languages.
limitations: The sampled paper uses limited project/domain coverage and the supplemental transfer papers have different data and evaluation protocols. This finding is primarily a synthesis and a guardrail against novelty overclaim; it is not a newly discovered transfer algorithm.
